claims.text: Homogenization at approximately 2100°C for 2 hours followed by rapid quenching will produce a refined, homogeneous microstructure.
The proposed treatment will produce a single-phase BCC state.
The proposed treatment will promote edge-dislocation-dominated plasticity.
The proposed treatment will improve elevated-temperature mechanical properties relative to the conventional as-cast state.
HfMoNbTaW and Ti2ZrHfxV0.5Ta0.2 are examples of low-activation refractory high-entropy alloys.
The relevant as-cast refractory HEAs exhibit compositional segregation or coarse microstructures.
The relevant as-cast refractory HEAs have limited high-temperature strength and softening resistance.
A short anneal after quenching can fine-tune the microstructure.
Testing at approximately 1600°C in an inert or vacuum atmosphere represents extreme aerospace or advanced-reactor service conditions.
The treatment will reduce segregation and minimize deleterious precipitate formation.
A refined, homogeneous single-phase BCC microstructure facilitates edge-dislocation motion.
High-temperature homogenization dissolves compositional inhomogeneities and potential precipitates.
Rapid quenching suppresses re-segregation after homogenization.
A uniform BCC matrix favors edge-dislocation slip over screw-dislocation slip at high temperatures.
Favoring edge-dislocation slip at high temperature leads to improved strength and reduced softening.
The treated alloy may have a 10–20% higher elevated-temperature yield strength than the as-cast alloy.
The conventional as-cast refractory HEA typically has elemental segregation and relies on less effective dislocation mechanisms at elevated temperatures.
The treatment benefit will be less pronounced in oxidizing atmospheres or at temperatures significantly below 1600°C.
